A city can be defined as a conditionally [contiguous](/wiki/Geographic_contiguity "Geographic contiguity") [urban area](/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area"), with relatively less regard to territorial or administrative boundaries. [UNICEF](/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF") defines urban area as follows:

> The definition of "urban" varies from country to country, and, with periodic reclassification, can also vary within one country over time, making direct comparisons difficult. An urban area can be defined by one or more of the following: administrative criteria or political boundaries (e.g., area within the jurisdiction of a municipality or town committee), a threshold population size (where the minimum for an urban settlement is typically in the region of 2,000 people, although this varies globally between 200 and 50,000), population density, economic function (e.g., where a significant majority of the population is not primarily engaged in agriculture, or where there is surplus employment) or the presence of urban characteristics (e.g., paved streets, electric lighting, sewerage).

According to [Demographia](/wiki/Demographia "Demographia"), an urban area is a continuously built up land mass of urban development that is within a labor market (metropolitan area or metropolitan region) and contains no [rural land](/wiki/Rural_area "Rural area").

For more variety of estimates, see [Megacity § List of megacities](/wiki/Megacity#List_of_megacities "Megacity").

There are 83 cities in the world with a population exceeding 5 million people, according to 2025 estimates by the [United Nations](/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[[11]](#cite_note-UNpopulation-11)

On April 15, *USA Today* launched a third international printing site, based in [Hong Kong](/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong"). Barnenez :: The monument :: Engraved symbols :: chunk_0004
Engraved symbols occur in several of the chambers and passages. They depict bows, axes, wave symbols or snakes and a repeated U-shaped sign. One of the carved slabs is in secondary use; it was originally part of a different structure, an interesting parallel to the situation in several other such monuments, including [Gavrinis](/wiki/Gavrinis "Gavrinis").

The symbols on the engraved blocks resemble those found in other megalithic monuments in Brittany; in broader terms they belong to the cultural phenomenon described as [megalithic art](/wiki/Megalithic_art "Megalithic art"). One of the recurring symbols is sometimes interpreted as an [anthropomorphic](/wiki/Anthropomorphic "Anthropomorphic") depiction (the so-called "Dolmen Goddess").

Only Cairn 2, namely chambers A, C and D, contained [Neolithic](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") finds at the time of excavation. They included pottery, polished stone axes (of [dolerite](/wiki/Dolerite "Dolerite")), [flint](/wiki/Flint "Flint") blades and arrowheads.

Pottery shards found outside the monument indicate that it was reused in the [Bronze Age](/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") (3rd millennium BC). A copper dagger and a barbed arrowhead are of [Chalcolithic](/wiki/Chalcolithic "Chalcolithic") date.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Similar, possibly contemporary, monuments are known at 22 other locations in France and on [Jersey](/wiki/Jersey "Jersey"). Breton examples are Larcuste-Colpo, Le Bono, Petit Mont, Ty-Floc´h, [Gavrinis](/wiki/Gavrinis "Gavrinis"), Île Carn, Ploudalmézeau and Guennoc (I´ile Gaignoc – sometimes spelt Guénioc) off the shore at [Landéda](/wiki/Land%C3%A9da "Landéda"). Those located on islands are generally better preserved. Chamber 3 B at Guennoc contains a small [standing stone](/wiki/Standing_stone "Standing stone") near the entrance.

An exhibition in the modern entrance building explains the results of scientific excavation and displays some objects from the site.
